results.name: trial_index_rating_correlation
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and rating; observed above the null means people drift toward saying yes more over the session, a time trend the stationary model does not produce (below means drift toward no).

results.name: shared_last_digit_contrast
results.description: In sets of 2+ examples that all end in the same digit, yes-rate for (non-identical) targets ending in that digit minus targets ending in another digit; observed above the null means people apply an explicit "ends in d" rule more sharply than the model's final-digit similarity dimension predicts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_contrast
# description: In sets of 2+ examples that all end in the same digit, yes-rate for (non-identical) targets ending in that digit minus targets ending in another digit; observed above the null means people apply an explicit "ends in d" rule more sharply than the model's final-digit similarity dimension predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).unique()
    dig = {}
    for s in sets:
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        ds = set(v % 10 for v in ex)
        dig[s] = (ds.pop() if (len(ex) >= 2 and len(ds) == 1) else -1)
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    d = ns.map(dig).values.astype(int)
    exs = ns.map({s: set(int(v) for v in s.split(",")) for s in sets})
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ident = np.array([tt in e for tt, e in zip(t, exs)])
    base = (d >= 0) & ~ident
    match = base & (t % 10 == d)
    other = base & (t % 10 != d)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if match.sum() == 0 or other.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[match].mean() - r[other].mean())

results.name: cell_response_dispersion
results.description: Mean over (number_set, target) cells of the within-cell Bernoulli variance p(1-p) of the repeated responses; observed below the null means people agree with each other on each item more (responses more deterministic/extreme) than the model's predicted probabilities imply, above means the model is overconfident.

results.name: interval_inside_minus_outside
results.description: In sets with 2+ examples, among targets not covered by a shared-factor rule (set gcd < 3 or target not a multiple of it) and not identical to an example, yes-rate for targets strictly inside the examples' [min,max] range minus targets outside it; observed above the null means people use an interval/range hypothesis more than the model's per-example similarity yields.
results.code:
# name: interval_inside_minus_outside
# description: In sets with 2+ examples, among targets not covered by a shared-factor rule (set gcd < 3 or target not a multiple of it) and not identical to an example, yes-rate for targets strictly inside the examples' [min,max] range minus targets outside it; observed above the null means people use an interval/range hypothesis more than the model's per-example similarity yields.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).unique()
    info = {}
    for s in sets:
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        g = 0
        for v in ex:
            g = math.gcd(g, v)
        info[s] = (len(ex), min(ex), max(ex), g, set(ex))
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    k = ns.map({s: v[0] for s, v in info.items()}).values
    lo = ns.map({s: v[1] for s, v in info.items()}).values
    hi = ns.map({s: v[2] for s, v in info.items()}).values
    g = ns.map({s: v[3] for s, v in info.items()}).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ident = np.array([tt in info[s][4] for tt, s in zip(t, ns.values)])
    gs = np.where(g >= 3, g, 1)
    covered = (g >= 3) & (t % gs == 0)
    base = (k >= 2) & ~ident & ~covered
    inside = base & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    outside = base & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if inside.sum() == 0 or outside.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[inside].mean() - r[outside].mean())

results.name: singleton_magnitude_gradient
results.description: For one-example sets (target not equal to the example), yes-rate for targets within 10 of the example minus yes-rate for targets more than 30 away; observed above the null means people's generalisation from a single example falls off with size distance more steeply than the model predicts, below means less steeply.
results.code:
# name: singleton_magnitude_gradient
# description: For one-example sets (target not equal to the example), yes-rate for targets within 10 of the example minus yes-rate for targets more than 30 away; observed above the null means people's generalisation from a single example falls off with size distance more steeply than the model predicts, below means less steeply.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~ns.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(ns.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    d = np.abs(t - x)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    s = single.values & (d > 0)
    near = s & (d <= 10)
    far = s & (d > 30)
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: identity_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials where the target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below the model's null means the model over-endorses already-seen examples (people reject some, e.g. 90/100 given 80,70,90,100), above means it under-endorses them.

results.name: shared_factor_nonmultiple_yes_rate
results.description: In sets of 2+ examples whose common factor g is >= 3, yes-rate for targets that are not multiples of g; observed above the null means the model's abstracted multiples-of-g rule rejects non-multiples too strongly (people still endorse them by similarity), below means not strongly enough.

results.name: power_of_two_set_contrast
results.description: In multi-example sets whose examples are all powers of two, yes-rate for power-of-two targets minus other targets (identity trials excluded); observed above the null means people abstract a "powers of 2" rule the model (which only has a multiples-of-g rule and graded factor similarity) under-produces.
results.code:
# name: power_of_two_set_contrast
# description: In multi-example sets whose examples are all powers of two, yes-rate for power-of-two targets minus other targets (identity trials excluded); observed above the null means people abstract a "powers of 2" rule the model (which only has a multiples-of-g rule and graded factor similarity) under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    p2 = {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).unique()
    ok = {}
    for s in sets:
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        ok[s] = len(ex) >= 2 and all(v in p2 for v in ex)
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    inset = ns.map(ok).astype(bool).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    exs = ns.map({s: set(int(v) for v in s.split(",")) for s in sets})
    ident = np.array([tt in e for tt, e in zip(t, exs)])
    tp2 = np.isin(t, list(p2))
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = inset & ~ident & tp2
    b = inset & ~ident & ~tp2
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
